blocks.text: Eco-Beige was a trend from the late 1980s that existed until about the mid-1990s. It is an eco-oriented aesthetic many businesses and brands adopted in an attempt to distance themselves from the gaudy excess of the 1980s and fit in to the new wave of environmental consciousness of the 1990s. It is characterized by its use of natural materials (like wood, straw, linens) or simple, handcrafted items.

Eco-Beige is a more brand-focused subsect of the broader Zen-X movement. The aesthetic emerged alongside the growing public interest in environmentalism of the 1990s, as brands began to change their look to appeal to the consumer and their newfound ideals: reusable materials, fair-trade practices, and an overall investment in conservationism and ecology. The look was intended to seem raw, unpretentious, and eco-friendly.

This aesthetic was frequently used as a way to covertly communicate a brand's environmental consciousness to consumers, regardless of whether a company had made corresponding changes to its materials, values or conduct. Businesses such as MUJI and Crate & Barrel, which focus on ethical production, safer materials/packaging, and sustainable sourcing, have incorporated understated, Eco-Beige interiors in their retail spaces. Conversely, retailers such as Urban Outfitters and its sister store, Free People still use the rustic, natural visuals of Eco-Beige without maintaining equivalent commitments to ethical practices or sustainable sourcing. This deceptive practice is called greenwashing, in which a company presents itself as more environmentally focused and friendly than they actually are.

During the 1990s, Eco-Beige was especially prevalent in the interiors of brick-and-mortar stores associated with natural and alternative consumer culture. Brands and retailers associated with the aesthetic include Origins, New Tee, J. Morgan Puett, and Anthropologie. These design elements were also common in spas, wellness-oriented businesses, and independent boutiques.

Although primarily found in commercial interiors, Eco-Beige also influenced fashion and home decor of the time. These applications similarly emphasized natural materials and colors, again reflecting the aesthetic's basis in the overarching Zen-X trend.

Visually, Eco-Beige comes off as rustic and naturalistic, sometimes even shabby. Through a soft, natural color palette, exposed surfaces, simple forms and an emphasis on raw materials, Eco-Beige creates an weathered, homespun atmosphere meant to convince viewers of its authenticity. Products are meant to seem hand-made and spaces are meant to feel stripped-down and real, rather than polished or highly curated. Materials commonly used to achieve this feeling include twigs, linen, wood, raffia straw, stones/pebbles, and exposed brick. Products made out of beeswax and bamboo, packaging made out of brown, unbleached paper, and items bound with dried grass, leaves or natural twine also contribute to the vibe. The colors most typically used in Eco-Beige are white and cream, orange, brown, green, muted blues, and of course, beige. Imagery within the aesthetic generally revolves around nature, and you'll most frequently see trees (and related materials such as bark, leaves, branches, pinecones and sticks), pressed botanicals, flowers, moss, seashells, honeycomb, fruits and vegetables, rocks and stones, and small creatures such as butterflies, bees, fish, and birds.

As mentioned above, critics of this aesthetic say that it is a vessel for company greenwashing, and enables businesses to feel and visually imply eco-friendliness without ever having to commit to actual eco-friendly practices or values.
